findings.title: New test depends on wall-clock time, making it flaky and weak
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which fixes both issued and now, test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls issue_token() and is_expired(token.expires_at) without an explicit 'now', so it depends on datetime.now(timezone.utc) at test-run time. The date() comparison on line 11 will intermittently fail if the test runs across a UTC midnight boundary, and because the token is issued and checked within the same instant, is_expired will pass trivially as long as the expiry window is not near-zero — it does not actually exercise the boundary condition the PR title claims to test ('the expiry window'). A real bug in the expiry threshold (e.g. off-by-a-day) could still pass this test as long as it runs well within the window.

findings.title: No test covers CouponExpired rejection path
findings.body: The PR's core behavior change—rejecting expired coupons by raising CouponExpired—has no test. The only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), which never exercises the new `if coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(...)` branch. findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; old callers omit it
findings.body: `apply_coupon` unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at`. The test change in this same PR shows that `Coupon(amount=10)` was previously a valid construction with no `expires_at`, so any caller or fixture that still builds a coupon that way now fails with `AttributeError` before reaching the discount logic. Either give `expires_at` a default on `Coupon` and treat the default (e.g. `None`) as "never expires", or guard the comparison: `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`. Please also confirm no production call site constructs coupons without the field.

findings.title: New CouponExpired branch has no test
findings.body: The only test exercises a coupon expiring tomorrow, so the new rejection path on lines 9–10 is never executed. Add a case asserting `pytest.raises(CouponExpired)` for a past `expires_at`, and ideally one at the exact boundary (`expires_at == now`) to pin down whether `<` or `<=` is intended — as written, a coupon expiring exactly now is still accepted.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside an async coroutine stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but its body contains no `await` — it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the thread running the event loop until the billing service responds or the 5s timeout fires. Every other request served by that loop is stalled for that window, so a slow `billing.internal` turns into a whole-process latency spike rather than one slow request.

Use the same async transport as the existing code path, e.g. accept/construct an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If a sync client is unavoidable, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` so it runs off the loop. Dropping the `requests` import (line 2) then keeps the module on a single HTTP stack.

findings.title: New async function using blocking requests.get is untested
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests` library, which will block the event loop during request handling. No test exercises this function, so a regression (or the underlying blocking-call defect itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id in URL path to internal billing service
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is interpolated raw into the request path for `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` does not encode `/`, `..` or `?` in an interpolated path segment, so a caller passing an attacker-supplied tenant identifier (e.g. from a request path or JSON body) could reach unrelated endpoints on the internal host — `../../admin/keys` collapses to `https://billing.internal/admin/keys`, and `1?admin=true` appends a query parameter. The host is internal, so this turns a tenant-scoped lookup into a limited SSRF against a service that is presumably not otherwise reachable from outside.

Fix by validating the identifier against its expected shape (UUID/integer) before use, or by passing it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same pattern exists on line 6 for the `httpx` call, so a shared validation helper at the boundary would cover both.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` (and `GeneratorExit`) are absorbed too — a Ctrl-C or a worker shutdown that lands inside `_client.send` will be silently turned into a normal `None` return instead of propagating. The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but no logging call was added, so every push failure — including programming errors like a `TypeError` from a malformed payload — disappears with no trace.

Narrow this to `except Exception:` and emit a log record, e.g. `logger.exception("metrics push failed")`, before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Telemetry failures silently swallowed with no log record

findings.title: No test exercises the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. No test file is included in this diff to verify that a failing send no longer raises, that None is returned, or that failures are logged as the PR description claims ('catch and log'). If this were reverted or broken (e.g., exception re-raised, or logging omitted), nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume races: reads counter, awaits, then writes without _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then yields to the event loop at `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 using the now-stale `current`. Two effects follow:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can all read the same `current`, all pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16, and all commit — total consumption becomes `current + N*cost`, arbitrarily above `LIMIT`.
2. **Lost updates.** The write on line 19 is an absolute assignment from a pre-await snapshot, not an increment. Any `consume()` (line 10) or `try_consume()` that completed during the suspension is silently overwritten, so the counter under-reports usage permanently.

`consume` already guards the same `_counters` dict with `_lock` (line 9), so this function is inconsistent with the established discipline for that state. Wrap the whole read-check-write in `async with _lock:`, and make the commit re-read and increment (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) rather than assign from the stale snapshot. If the `await` is not needed, drop it too.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter outside the lock

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrency/race behavior
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant, 0) outside of _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point), then writes _counters[tenant] without holding the lock. This is a classic check-then-act race: two concurrent calls can both read the same 'current' value, both pass the limit check, and both write, letting a tenant exceed LIMIT. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch this race or even verify the basic accept/reject behavior of try_consume. At minimum, a test should assert that concurrent try_consume calls near the limit never allow the total to exceed LIMIT, and a basic test should confirm try_consume returns False once cost would exceed LIMIT and True otherwise.

findings.title: Docstring says '(name, email)' but function now returns a dict
findings.body:
The docstring `"""Return (name, email) for a user."""` still promises a 2-tuple, but the function body now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. A caller reading only the docstring (e.g. `reports/weekly.py`'s `render_row`, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) would reasonably expect a tuple and break at runtime. Update the docstring to reflect the new dict return shape and its keys.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`. It now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict yields its keys, so this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even with two keys it would silently bind key strings rather than values.

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's breaking return-shape change
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple. The retrieved repository context shows reports/weekly.py:render_row does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise (unpacking a dict yields keys, not the expected two values, and if there are 3 keys it will fail outright) once this change ships. findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding insert failures
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to a new `err` scoped to the `if` statement on line 15; it is logged but never propagated. Lines 18-19 then declare a fresh, always-nil `err` and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the INSERT fails.

The signature returns `error`, and line 12-14 already propagates the validation error, so callers will reasonably read a nil return as "settlement persisted". In an end-of-day batch that means dropped settlement rows are reported as success and never retried or reconciled.

If per-row failures really should not abort the batch, that decision belongs to the caller: return the insert error here (`return err` inside the `if`, or `return fmt.Errorf("insert settlement %v: %w", s.ID, err)`) and let the batch loop log-and-continue. If this function genuinely must never fail on insert, it should not advertise an `error` return, or should at minimum be documented as best-effort.

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` on line 18 and returns it unconditionally, so the function always returns nil even when the db.Exec insert on line 15 fails (only a log line is emitted). There is no test exercising WriteSettlement with a failing db.Exec, so this always-succeeds behavior would not be caught by any existing check. Add a test that forces the insert to fail and asserts the returned error is non-nil.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` is shared and returned across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument mutates and returns the *same* list object. The second call to `send_with_retries(...)` will return the failures from the first call plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Callers that inspect the return value to decide what failed will see stale recipients, and because the same object is returned, a caller holding a reference from an earlier call will see it mutate underneath them.

Fix with the standard sentinel pattern:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
    ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared default list leaks recipients across calls in send_with_retries

findings.title: send_with_retries mutable default arg has no test to catch state leakage
findings.body: send_with_retries uses `attempted=[]` as a default argument, which is shared across calls and will accumulate recipients from previous invocations that didn't pass an explicit list. No test exists for this function at all, so a call sequence like `send_with_retries(['a'])` followed by `send_with_retries(['b'])` returning `['a','b']` instead of `['b']` would go undetected.

findings.title: Rounding threshold silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
Every other function in this diff is a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes its comparison operator: the old `calc_rounding` returned 1 when `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5`, the new one only when `> 0.5`. A line with a remainder of exactly 0.5 cents now rounds down instead of up, changing monetary totals for a reachable and common input (half-cent remainders are precisely what a rounding helper exists to resolve). If this behaviour change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test and a note in the PR description; if not, restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > during rename

findings.title: page_of_sorted drops one record per page (off-by-one slice)
findings.body:
`ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items, while `start` advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is therefore returned by no page at all — for every page requested, exactly one record is silently omitted from the export. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct bound `start + PAGE_SIZE`; the new function should match it:

    return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]

Because this is an export path, the failure is silent data loss rather than an error: callers paging through all pages will believe they have a complete dump.

findings.title: New page_of_sorted has no test and contains an off-by-one slice
findings.body: page_of_sorted slices ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1], which returns one fewer record than PAGE_SIZE per page — records get silently dropped from export output. findings.title: Dropped None guard makes header_lines raise for most invoices

`Invoice.purchase_order` is declared `str | None` and the model docstring states it is only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). findings.title: No test covers header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: The repository model docs state purchase_order is optional and unset for ~95% of customers, but the guard that handled that case was removed. There is no test in this diff exercising header_lines with invoice.purchase_order=None, so nothing would catch the AttributeError this now raises for the common case.

findings.title: File handle leaked when header validation fails or read raises
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is not managed by a context manager, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When `header != expected_header` the function returns on line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) — e.g. `csv.Error` on a malformed row, `UnicodeDecodeError` on bad encoding — escapes without closing either. Rewrite using `with open(path) as fh:` around the whole body, matching `read_rows` on lines 5-6.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() — duplicate charges on transient failure
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. That function's own docstring states "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and points at the gateway's `Idempotency-Key` header as the mechanism for making retries safe. No key is generated or passed here, so a timeout or 5xx after the gateway has already accepted the POST will cause the retry to create a second (and possibly third) charge against the customer's card — money moved twice, with no way for the caller to detect it.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. accept one as a parameter or derive it from the order/payment id) and thread it through `gateway.charge` so all three attempts share the same key. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards that key, the retry decorator should be removed from this path. The retry on `fetch_charge` (line 5) is fine — `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat.

There is no test verifying that a retried charge_card call does not produce multiple charges (e.g. a test that simulates a transient failure after the gateway actually created the charge, then asserts only one charge exists/no duplicate POST occurs). Without such a test, a change that makes this worse (or a review that misses the missing idempotency key) would pass silently.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails for every input — the function can never return. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (Note also that with naive local time the comparison would silently be off by the UTC offset rather than erroring, if the host is not UTC.) findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms; articles silently unfindable
findings.body: `upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly warns that it does not normalise: a cased term creates a separate posting list that lower-casing queries will never hit, so the document indexes "successfully" but is silently unfindable by that term. `article.title.split()` returns the title's words verbatim — titles are typically capitalised, so most terms land under the wrong key and the failure is silent (no exception, no log). findings.title: Referer is logged unscrubbed, leaking auth tokens into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging it. With that gone, line 5 writes the raw header into the log on every 5xx. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and the browser echoes that URL back in `Referer` on every subresource request — so the logged value will routinely contain a live auth token. Anyone with read access to the server logs (or a log-shipping pipeline) gains the ability to authenticate as the user.

Restore the scrubbing for `Referer` (and keep any other URI-bearing headers scrubbed). If the goal was simply to see more of what the client sent, scrub the token parameter and log the rest. Note also that dropping the only use of `extra_param_keys` likely leaves that parameter dead in this function's signature, which is a hint that the removal was unintentional.

Removing `xlinkhref` from that condition means the value falls through to whatever the default branch does and is no longer scheme-checked. `xlink:href` is a live navigation sink inside SVG: `` executes in browsers that still honour the XLink namespace, and `xlink:href` on ``/`` is equally a URL sink. findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets `project` query param traverse out of the storage root
findings.body:
`query.GetProjectQueryParam()` is unauthenticated, fully attacker-controlled request data. The removed `common.ValidateID` call was the only check constraining it to an identifier shape; after this change the raw string flows onward to the file DAO, whose `buildPath` does `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` and explicitly documents "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point."

`filepath.Join` does not confine its result to the first argument — it cleans the path, so a value like `../../../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`. An unauthenticated caller can therefore read (and, on write paths sharing the same helper, create/overwrite) documents outside the project sandbox, and at minimum can read another tenant's project regardless of the path-scoped authorization implied by `parameters.Project`.

The PR description's premise — "the path join already scopes under the folder root" — is incorrect for `filepath.Join`. Restore the `ValidateID` check here, or make `buildPath` reject names containing separators/`..` (e.g. reject if the cleaned absolute path is not under `d.Folder`).

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-controlled Content-Length (memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` is the declared length of the uploaded part, i.e. it comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header on the S3 UploadPart request; it is not a measured byte count. Passing it to `Reserve` makes the server commit that much memory *before* reading a single byte, so a client that sends `Content-Length: 50000000000` with an empty or slow body causes a multi-gigabyte allocation (and, with a handful of concurrent requests, OOM of the rclone process). The previous code grew the pool-backed RW as bytes actually arrived, which bounded memory by bytes actually delivered.

Suggested fix: clamp the reservation to the configured maximum part/chunk size and to a sane absolute ceiling, e.g. `rw := multipart.NewRW(); if contentLength > 0 { rw.Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize)) }`, and reject the request up-front when `contentLength` exceeds the allowed part size. Also guard the `contentLength < 0` (unknown/chunked) case, which should not reach `Reserve` at all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Part buffer sized from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or mismatch handling
findings.body: The change pre-allocates the multipart RW buffer using the declared contentLength. There is no test in this diff verifying that: (1) the reserved capacity matches the actual bytes written when contentLength is accurate, (2) behavior when contentLength disagrees with actual body size (too small/too large), or (3) that a large/untrusted contentLength doesn't cause excessive allocation. If Reserve() is buggy or if contentLength is attacker-controlled and unbounded, nothing here would fail — the function would still compile and the happy-path callers would still pass silently.

findings.title: Unknown/negative contentLength is passed straight to Reserve
findings.body: Go's HTTP stack reports `ContentLength == -1` for chunked or otherwise unknown-length bodies, and this function's `contentLength int64` parameter can carry that value through. Line 6 forwards it to `Reserve` with no guard. Depending on `Reserve`'s implementation this either panics on a negative make/grow size or silently no-ops — neither is checked here. Guard with `if contentLength > 0` before reserving.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently flips from https to http
findings.body:
The previous expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` selected plaintext **only** when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common one where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`.

The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` tests truthiness, so `None` (key absent) now yields `http`. Line 6 then builds `http://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com{path}`, sending the request — and any AWS signature/authorization headers attached to it — over an unencrypted connection by default. Other falsy-but-not-False values (`0`, `""`) change behaviour the same way.

To keep the semantics while simplifying, use an explicit default: `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged), or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression treated a missing `is_secure` key as secure: only an explicit `False` produced `http`. The new ternary is falsy-based, so `request.meta.get("is_secure")` returning `None` (key absent — the normal case for any request that did not explicitly opt in) now yields `scheme = "http"`, and that scheme is interpolated straight into the request URL on line 6.

Adversary: any on-path network observer (shared Wi-Fi, upstream ISP, compromised router, a proxy in the chain). What they control: nothing — passive observation suffices; an active MITM gets more. What they get: the full S3 request in cleartext, including the AWS `Authorization`/signature headers used to authenticate the fetch, plus the object bytes in the response. A captured signed request can be replayed until its expiry, and an active attacker can substitute response content that then gets parsed by the spider.

Restore the secure-by-default semantics, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make the default explicit: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.body: The scheme-selection logic changed its default behavior: previously, when `is_secure` was absent or None, the code defaulted to `https`; now it defaults to `http`. This is a meaningful behavior change (plaintext vs encrypted transport) with no test in this diff exercising the case where `is_secure` is not explicitly set to True/False. If this logic regresses again, nothing shown here would fail.

findings.title: DELETE requests now authorised as "push", bypassing delete permission
findings.body:
The removed `switch` mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the new two-branch form maps every non-GET/HEAD method — including DELETE — to `push`. The resulting `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` is the value the access-control layer checks, so a DELETE on a repository is now approved by a push grant.

Entry point: the HTTP request method and the `name` mux var on the registry endpoint. Sink: `requestedAccess` on line 9, consumed by the per-repository authorisation check. Adversary: any authenticated account provisioned with push-only access (e.g. a CI publishing token). What they control: the verb on a request to a repo they can push to. What they get: destruction of existing tags/manifests they were explicitly not granted `delete` on — and after this change no code path can ever produce the `delete` action, so a delete-denying policy becomes unenforceable.

Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if` arm) before the catch-all push assignment.

The new condition treats everything that is not GET/HEAD as `"push"`, so such requests now demand write access. If the registry serves CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) or any read-ish verb anonymously, those requests will start failing authorization. If the intent was to preserve the old default, the condition needs to enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

This diff collapses HTTP DELETE into the "push" action instead of "delete", so the documented invariant no longer matches the code: granting push now also grants the ability to delete, contrary to what the comment promises callers/operators configuring access.

This diff includes no test asserting the action computed for http.MethodDelete, so a revert or further regression of this authorization logic would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: Overflow handling clears the whole cache, discarding the just-fetched entry
findings.body: When `_CACHE` crosses 1000 entries, the entire dictionary is cleared — including the entry written one line earlier on line 10. The caller of `get_tenant_fresh` still gets its value back, but every other tenant (and the one just refreshed) is evicted, so the next round of `get_tenant` calls all return `None` at once. On a busy cache this turns a size bound into a periodic full-cache stampede, and it is also a check-then-act on shared mutable state: a concurrent `get_tenant` can observe the cache emptied between the write on line 10 and its own read. Prefer bounded eviction (e.g. drop the oldest entry, or use an LRU such as `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`) rather than `clear()`, and do the size check before inserting so the fresh value survives.

get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug in the fetch call, the cache write, or the eviction threshold (e.g. off-by-one, wrong comparison, clearing on every call) would not be caught.

findings.title: A `None`/failed result from `_fetch` is cached and served by `get_tenant`

If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown or temporarily unavailable tenant, that negative result is now indistinguishable from a cache miss in `get_tenant` (line 5 returns `None` for both) and will be served until the cache happens to be cleared. findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id can force a full cache flush (amplification DoS)

`get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry keyed by the caller-supplied `tenant_id` before checking size, and the overflow policy is `_CACHE.clear()` — dropping every entry, not just the new one. If any request-handling path reaches this function with a tenant_id the caller influences (including ids that do not exist, since the result of `_fetch` is stored unconditionally), roughly 1000 cheap calls wipe the cache for every tenant, forcing a stampede of `_fetch` calls from all other traffic. Consider bounding growth with an LRU eviction of a single entry (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an `OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) and not caching misses, so one caller cannot evict everyone else's data.

Adversary: any client that can reach a handler passing a tenant_id through to this helper. What they control: the key, and how often they call. What they get: repeated global cache invalidation and the backend load that follows. I could not establish the entry point — no caller is present in the diff or in the retrieved context — so the confidence reflects that the exploitability depends on unseen code.

findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this file uses the explicit relative form (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a top-level module named `adapters`, which does not exist on the path when `requests` is installed; under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` on `import requests`.
